For any two elements \(V\) and \(r\) the “multiplication’’ is  

\[
V*r \;:=\; V(x^{2})\;\bigl(r(x/3)\bigr),
\]

i.e. evaluate the first polynomial at \(x^{2}\) and the second polynomial at \(x/3\), then multiply the two results.

---

**Step 2 – Compute \((f*K)\)**  

\[
f*K \;=\; f(x^{2})\;K\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right).
\]

Denote this intermediate polynomial by  

\[
P(x)=f(x^{2})\,K\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right).
\]

---

**Step 3 – Compute \((f*K)*b\)**  

Now treat \(P\) as the first factor and \(b\) as the second:

\[
(f*K)*b \;=\; P(x^{2})\;b\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)
           \;=\; \bigl[f(x^{2})\,K\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\bigr]_{x\to x^{2}}\;
                b\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right).
\]

Since \(P(x^{2})=f(x^{4})\,K\!\left(\frac{x^{2}}{3}\right)\),

\[
\boxed{(f*K)*b \;=\; f(x^{4})\,K\!\left(\frac{x^{2}}{3}\right)\,b\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)}.
\]

---

**Step 4 – Compute \((K*b)\)**  

\[
K*b \;=\; K(x^{2})\;b\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)=:Q(x).
\]

---

**Step 5 – Compute \(f*(K*b)\)**  

Now use \(f\) as the first factor and \(Q\) as the second:

\[
f*(K*b) \;=\; f(x^{2})\;Q\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)
           \;=\; f(x^{2})\;
               \Bigl[K(x^{2})\,b\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\Bigr]_{x\to x/3}.
\]

Evaluating \(Q\) at \(x/3\) gives  

\[
Q\!\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)=K\!\left(\frac{x^{2}}{9}\right)\,
                            b\!\left(\frac{x}{9}\right).
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{f*(K*b) \;=\; f(x^{2})\,
                     K\!\left(\frac{x^{2}}{9}\right)\,
                     b\!\left(\frac{x}{9}\right)}.
\]

---

**Step 6 – Compare the two results**  

The two expressions are

\[
\begin{aligned}
L &:= (f*K)*b = f(x^{4})\,K\!\bigl(\tfrac{x^{2}}{3}\bigr)\,b\!\bigl(\tfrac{x}{3}\bigr),\\[4pt]
R &:= f*(K*b) = f(x^{2})\,K\!\bigl(\tfrac{x^{2}}{9}\bigr)\,b\!\bigl(\tfrac{x}{9}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

In general these polynomials are **different** (they have different degrees, different coefficients, etc.).  

To see this concretely, pick simple polynomials, e.g.  

\[
f(x)=x+1,\qquad K(x)=x+2,\qquad b(x)=x+3.
\]

Then  

\[
\begin{aligned}
L(x) &= \tfrac{1}{9}x^{7}+x^{6}+\tfrac{2}{3}x^{5}+6x^{4}
      +\tfrac{1}{9}x^{3}+x^{2}+\tfrac{2}{3}x+6,\\[2pt]
R(x) &= \tfrac{1}{81}x^{5}+\tfrac{1}{3}x^{4}
      +\tfrac{19}{81}x^{3}+\tfrac{19}{3}x^{2}
      +\tfrac{2}{9}x+6.
\end{aligned}
\]

Clearly \(L\neq R\).

---

**Step 7 – Apply the equality operator “\(=\)”**  

The definition says  

\[
\Psi = A \iff \text{(sum of the roots of }\Psi(x)\text{)}=
            \text{(sum of the roots of }A(x)\text{)} .
\]

For a polynomial \(p(x)=a_nx^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots +a_0\) the sum of its roots is \(-a_{n-1}/a_n\).

* For \(L\): leading coefficient \(a_7=\tfrac{1}{9}\), next coefficient \(a_6=1\).

* For \(R\): leading coefficient \(a_5=\tfrac{1}{81}\), next coefficient \(a_4=\tfrac13\).

Since \(-9\neq-27\), the equality \(L=R\) does **not** hold.
